chapter_theme: In the council hall the counsellors name the princes who might win the maiden, and the sarukkam closes on Pavachchuthan's judgment, the gifts of Suthasagaran and a warning about the danger of the match.

cast.role: the counsellors who name the suitors; the speaker of most verses is read as one of them
the king who names his heir to the city
a learned counsellor whose word settles the choice
the man who brings the gifts to the chosen prince

311.reading: The speaker says the woman who takes the queen's crown beside the lord of the flowered shore is like Lakshmi herself, praised by all the others sent to wear the title.
311.nuance: The grammar of lines 1-3 is compressed and the queen meant is not named; the verse is read as praise of a chief queen at a court.

312.reading: The speaker says the son who came as the good child of our lord and, by his lord's order, became the young king, is praised by the world as a lord of the just sceptre who enjoys its pleasure.
312.nuance: Who the young king is cannot be fixed from these lines; the 'just sceptre' praise is the speaker's.

313.reading: The speaker says that a palm-leaf horoscope was written for the maiden, and that, now she has reached the age of desire, the prince who will be her helper stands near.
313.nuance: The leaf is the first sign in the chapter that her match is fixed by a written fate and not by choice; whether the leaf names a man is not stated.
313.event: A horoscope leaf written for the maiden is recalled, and the one who is to be her partner is said to be at hand.

314.reading: The speaker says that, by the saying that the aeon's time has run out for Achuvakandan the lord of the sea-girt earth, the maiden with the flowery eyes will not be found for any other.
314.nuance: ஊழிக் காலம் ஓடின can be read as a foretelling of the king's end; it returns at 333 where the words said of him are matched with old saying. The sense is held open.

315.reading: The speaker names the king's beloved Sittirai as the maiden of golden fame, who holds the queen's crown with the grace of her gentle beauty.
315.nuance: 'Sittirai' is read as a woman's name; the line is compressed.

316.reading: The speaker says that among the five hundred sons of the king, Ratnakandan stands before them and is the young king of all the others, bright as a shining spear.
316.nuance: The last line is tangled; the praise of Ratnakandan is the sure part.
316.event: Ratnakandan is named the chief among five hundred princes.

317.reading: The king declares that this one is who he will be to him and rules this city, and so he makes known to the whole city who the heir is.
317.event: The king announces the heir to the whole city.

318.reading: A speaker addressing the chief of the great hill asks that the lady be given to the one among the youths with sharp spears who is truly worthy of her.
318.nuance: Verses 318-329 are a list of names and lands: the speaker is read as a counsellor, but the Tamil gives no word for his office.
318.event: The speaker begins to name the princes and asks that the maiden be given to the worthy one.

319.reading: The counsellor names Pavananjan, son of the king on the Kinnara hill and a master of horses, as a young prince for her to consider.
319.event: A prince of the hill, Pavananjan, is put forward.

320.reading: The counsellor puts forward the son of the king of Amirthamapati, Vegaman of firm shoulders, whom the whole earth praises as a young lion.

321.reading: The counsellor names the son of the king of Megamapuram, Pathumatheran, whom kings fear as the fire of the aeon.

322.reading: The counsellor names the grandson of the king of Rathinapuram, a noble youth who is like thunder under cloud.
322.event: A grandson of the king of Rathinapuram is put forward.

323.reading: The counsellor says that Arikandan, son of the king of the city Keetham, rules a great earth, and not even the red-eyed Tirumal in anger could do him harm.
323.nuance: செங்கண்மான் is the epic's own epithet for its hero (verse 2, the red-eyed tall one), so the boast sits beside the story's turn.
323.event: Arikandan is put forward and said to be unassailable.

324.reading: The counsellor names the son of the king of Thiripuram, Alithangan, as a bull among warrior kings, hot as fire and deep in learning as the sea.

325.reading: The counsellor says the son of the king of Chitrakuta is like Indra's son, so that the kings who live in this world of mantra are no match for him.
325.nuance: The name of the prince in line 3 is read from compressed grammar; the Indra comparison is clear.

326.reading: The counsellor names Kanakachitran, son of the king of Achuvapuram, and says that the earth owns him as its one jewel for the forehead.

327.reading: The counsellor names the grandson of the king of Sirinilai, Chitrattheran, as one who will be the single mark of beauty on the whole earth.
327.event: A prince of Sirinilai is put forward.

328.reading: The counsellor names Singakethu, son of the king of Kanakapallavam, who crushes the pride of his foes, and says the earth rejoiced after his birth.

329.reading: The counsellor names Arunjayan, son of Sanjayan, before whom all the earth trembles, and says he is to the hills as the crest-jewel.
329.event: Arunjayan, son of Sanjayan, is put forward; the roll of suitors ends.

330.reading: A speaker asks that the young man worthy of the maiden be sought out from among these princes, examined and told to him, in words like gems cast up by the sea.
330.nuance: The speaker is not named; he may be the king or the one who has just read the roll.
330.event: The speaker asks that the worthy prince be examined and chosen from the list.

331.reading: Pavachchuthan of wide learning speaks briefly to the one whose feet are served by kings' crowns, and all present agree that it is so.
331.nuance: What Pavachchuthan said is not given in the verse.
331.event: Pavachchuthan gives the judgment and the whole company agrees to it.

332.reading: Suthasagaran brings a flower garland, a string of pearls, a fruit-bearing creeper and sandal paste, and says something to the wrestler of the broad chest.
332.nuance: The words are not quoted; that these are betrothal gifts is likely but is the reader's inference.
332.event: Suthasagaran speaks to the chosen man and gives him garlands, pearls and sandal.

333.reading: The speaker tells the lord with the crested elephant that the words said about Achuvakandan, who rules the sea-girt earth, and Pavachchuthan, the strong-shouldered, are like the old words of the aeon.
333.nuance: ஊழியார் உரை recalls 314 (ஊழிக் காலம் ஓடின). Whether it means the elders' fate-lore or a prophecy is not fixed.

334.reading: The speaker says there is a little knowledge in what he reports, but that even the soft arms of the flower-garlanded girl would turn to enmity if others touched them, and so the bright-speared one should take care.
334.nuance: This verse ends the section on a warning that undoes the praise of the list; the line has hard compounds.

links.note: Verse 314 speaks of the aeon's time running out for Achuvakandan; verse 333 says the words spoken of him match the old words of the aeon.
links.teaches: The council's reasoning comes back to the same fated end, so the choice of a husband is set under a doom the epic has already spoken.

links.note: Verse 323 claims no one, not even the red-eyed Tirumal in anger, can harm Arikandan; verse 2 says the tale is of the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion.
links.teaches: The boast of an unassailable prince is held against the hero the poet promised at the start, so a reader hears the council's confidence as a setup for its overturning.

links.note: Kural 504 says to examine qualities and faults and take what predominates; the roll of princes names only qualities, and verse 334 ends on a danger.
links.teaches: The council's list of suitors names only merits and the last verse adds a warning, which shows the Kural's rule to weigh faults was missing from the roll.

gains.a: A named rule by which the one-sided praise of the roll is judged and found short.
gains.b: A court scene in which the praise-only roll of candidates is the failure it warns of.

links.note: Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes, to be taken after counsel; verse 330 asks that the worthy suitor be examined and then Pavachchuthan's word settles it.
links.teaches: The epic shows counsel working as the Kural wants, by examining before choosing, but one man's word still carries the room.

gains.a: A standard that says who should do the examining and why his word is valued.
gains.b: A scene in which the eyes of the king are tested by a real choice and the room simply agrees.

source_issues: Verses 311-317: the Tamil gives no clear speaker and the verses are written in compressed grammar; the speaker is taken as a counsellor and every verse is flagged uncertain.
Verse 320 line 3 repaired; verse 333 line 2 repaired (stray space before a dead consonant).
Verse 329 ends with an exclamation mark that the edition added.
